title: Understanding Teacher Revisions of Large Language Model-Generated Feedback
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how teachers revise large language model (LLM)-generated formative feedback before it is delivered to students. The authors focus on a practical but under-studied question in AI-supported education: when AI feedback is produced for classroom use, do teachers accept it, edit it, or rewrite it, and what does that reveal about the fit between model output and instructional needs? The study is especially relevant to concerns about pedagogical misalignment, overexplanatory feedback, and the degree to which teachers actually mediate AI output in practice.

The intervention/approach studied is a co-creation workflow in the Tutoria platform, where an LLM drafts feedback on short open-ended student responses and teachers can accept, edit, or fully rewrite the feedback. The analysis uses 1,349 feedback instances from 117 teachers, drawing from Brazilian high school chemistry contexts, introductory computer science in higher education, and related extracurricular classroom deployments. The researchers quantify textual changes, predict which drafts will be revised using text-only machine learning models, and qualitatively code how pedagogical feedback types shift from AI draft to final teacher message.

Results show that teachers accepted AI feedback unchanged in about 78%–80% of cases, and many teachers rarely edited at all; however, a small subset revised frequently. When revisions occurred, teachers usually shortened the feedback while preserving most of its meaning, suggesting compression rather than wholesale correction. Teachers also often shifted feedback away from more explanatory high-information forms toward more concise corrective forms, indicating that verbosity and pedagogical framing can trigger intervention. Overall, the paper concludes that default AI behavior is instructionally consequential because most drafts are delivered unchanged, and that AI feedback tools should better align with teacher priorities while reducing unnecessary editing effort.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic large language model / generative AI system used to draft formative feedback for students, later revised by teachers.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies AI-generated formative feedback drafts produced by LLMs in the Tutoria platform and how teachers revise, accept, shorten, or rewrite those drafts before delivery to students.

findings.finding_summary: Across 1,349 feedback instances from 117 teachers, teachers accepted AI feedback without modification in 77.8% of cases (1050/1349). Revised feedback was only modestly longer than unedited feedback (48.3 vs. 41.9 words within-teacher difference = 6.4 words, p=.024), suggesting most teacher edits were limited rather than full rewrites.
findings.measure: Teacher acceptance/edit rate and feedback length

findings.finding_summary: Teachers often simplified AI-generated feedback, shifting it away from high-information explanations toward more concise corrective forms. findings.finding_summary: Text-only models could predict which AI feedback would be revised above chance, but only modestly. Holdout ROC AUC ranged from 0.698 to 0.746 across models, with overlapping confidence intervals and close-to-modest Cohen's ba values.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods observational study using retrospective log data, descriptive statistics, predictive modeling, and qualitative coding rather than an experimental design. It provides useful evidence on teacher mediation of LLM feedback, but causal claims are limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The most concrete effect is operational: teachers accepted most AI feedback unchanged, and revisions were usually small. The reported behavioral shifts are modest in magnitude (e.g., Cram�e9r�e2s V=0.12), so the practical impact appears limited but real.
